summary.title: Characteristics of EGRET Blazars in the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS)
summary.authors: G. B. Taylor, S. E. Healey, J. F. Helmboldt, S. Tremblay, C. D. Fassnacht, R. C. Walker, L. O. Sjouwerman, T. J. Pearson, A. C. S. Readhead, L. Weintraub, N. Gehrels, R. W. Romani, P. F. Michelson, R. D. Blandford, G. Cotter
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the radio properties of blazars detected by the EGRET instrument on the Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory, utilizing data from the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS). VIPS provides a uniform sample of 1127 flat-spectrum sources with a flux limit significantly lower than previous surveys like MOJAVE, allowing for a more unbiased comparison between gamma-ray loud and quiet blazars. The authors compare 31 EGRET candidate blazars within the VIPS field to the broader VIPS population. The primary finding is that at lower radio flux levels, radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux density. Instead, EGRET-detected blazars exhibit distinct morphological and physical characteristics: they tend to have higher core brightness temperatures, greater core fractions (indicating more core-dominated emission), and possibly larger jet opening angles. A weak correlation is also observed with jet length and polarization. These trends are interpreted as evidence for systematically larger Doppler factors in gamma-ray loud blazars, implying that their jets are oriented closer to the line of sight. This beaming effect explains the enhanced radio properties and is consistent with previous monitoring programs that found higher apparent velocities in these sources. The paper concludes that selecting sources for future gamma-ray studies, such as those with the GLAST telescope, should prioritize high core fractions, high brightness temperatures, and large opening angles rather than just radio brightness. The study highlights the importance of multi-wavelength monitoring and VLBI polarimetry to discriminate between different gamma-ray production mechanisms in active galactic nuclei.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the radio properties of blazars detected by the EGRET instrument on the Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory, utilizing data from the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS). VIPS provides a uniform sample of 1127 flat-spectrum sources with a flux limit significantly lower than previous surveys like MOJAVE, allowing for a more unbiased comparison between gamma-ray loud and quiet blazars. The authors compare 31 EGRET candidate blazars within the VIPS field to the broader VIPS population. The primary finding is that at lower radio flux levels, radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux density. Instead, EGRET-detected blazars exhibit distinct morphological and physical characteristics: they tend to have higher core brightness temperatures, greater core fractions (indicating more core-dominated emission), and possibly larger jet opening angles. A weak correlation is also observed with jet length and polarization. These trends are interpreted as evidence for systematically larger Doppler factors in gamma-ray loud blazars, implying that their jets are oriented closer to the line of sight. This beaming effect explains the enhanced radio properties and is consistent with previous monitoring programs that found higher apparent velocities in these sources. The paper concludes that selecting sources for future gamma-ray studies, such as those with the GLAST telescope, should prioritize high core fractions, high brightness temperatures, and large opening angles rather than just radio brightness. The study highlights the importance of multi-wavelength monitoring and VLBI polarimetry to discriminate between different gamma-ray production mechanisms in active galactic nuclei.

Research Context
At high galactic latitudes, most EGRET sources are identified with blazars. These blazars exhibit flat radio spectra and superluminal motion. Previous studies suggested EGRET flares lagged behind mm flares. Other studies claimed enhanced radio emission following gamma-ray activity. Lister & Homan found EGRET blazars have more polarized jets. Kovalev et al. reported EGRET blazars were more compact. It remains unclear if radio flaring precedes or follows gamma-ray flares. The VIPS survey provides a uniform sample for study.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study examines correlations in parsec-scale jet properties of EGRET blazars. The hypothesis is that EGRET blazars have higher Doppler factors. This would manifest as larger core fractions and brightness temperatures. The authors predict a lack of direct radio-gamma flux correlation. They hypothesize that gamma-ray selected sources are more beamed. The study tests if EGRET blazars have larger jet opening angles. It investigates if EGRET blazars have longer jets on average. The goal is to understand the selection bias in gamma-ray samples.

Methodological Details
The study uses the 5 GHz VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey. VIPS observed 1127 flat-spectrum sources stronger than 85 mJy. The survey covers the Northern Cap region of SDSS. The sample includes 958 full polarization images. The EGRET sample consists of 173 candidate sources. The VIPS sample contains 31 EGRET candidate blazars. Sources are classified as likely or plausible based on Figure of Merit. Likely candidates have a FoM greater than 1. Plausible candidates have a FoM between 0.25 and 1.0. The comparison population is the full VIPS survey of 1127 sources. Brightness temperatures were derived from automatic model fits. Jet opening angles were measured using component separations.

Procedures And Architectures
The VIPS survey was carried out between January and August 2006. Images were created at 5 GHz for VIPS sources. MOJAVE images at 15 GHz were used for 6 sources. Source classification used an automatic scheme from Helmboldt et al. Classes include PS, SJET, LJET, CSO, and CPLX. Core fraction is the ratio of core to jet flux density. Brightness temperature was calculated using core flux and size. Jet opening angle was calculated using arctan of perpendicular distance. Jet bending was calculated by fitting a parabola to centroids. K-S tests were used to compare distributions between samples.

Key Results
Radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux. EGRET blazars have higher brightness temperatures than the VIPS average. The K-S test probability for brightness temperature is 4%. EGRET blazars have greater core fractions. The K-S test probability for core fraction is 4%. Polarization is detected in 48% of EGRET candidates. This is higher than the 36% average in VIPS. There is a marginally significant excess of long jets. 3 sources have jet opening half-angles exceeding the VIPS median. The probability of this occurring by chance is less than 1 in 3. There is no appreciable difference in jet length distributions. The K-S probability for jet length is 34%.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results support models where gamma-rays are produced in a jet. The jet is oriented at a small angle to the line-of-sight. This implies systematically larger Doppler factors in EGRET blazars. Higher Doppler factors explain higher core fractions and temperatures. It also explains higher polarization and faster motions. The large opening angles suggest a sight-line within the beaming cone. Gamma rays are likely more tightly beamed than radio emission. This selection effect naturally explains the observed radio properties.

Contradictions And Limitations
The sample size for polarization is too small for definitive statements. There is a mix of 5 GHz and 15 GHz measurements. Only 4 EGRET/VIPS sources have enough components for unbiased analysis. The statistics for jet opening angles are poor. The evidence for long jets is of marginal significance. The redshift distribution for the VIPS sample is incomplete. It is difficult to investigate possible selection bias at this time. Some sources may be composites of multiple blazars.

Claims
EGRET blazars have systematically larger Doppler factors than the general radio-selected population. They have higher brightness temperatures. They have greater core fractions. They have higher polarization. Piner et al. found no significant difference in jet velocities. Gamma-ray selected sources are more beamed. Selection for future studies should use core properties.
Radio flux density is not a reliable predictor of gamma-ray flux density at low flux levels. VIPS has a flux limit an order of magnitude lower. No direct correlation was found. Previous studies claimed enhanced radio emission after gamma-ray activity. Selecting brightest radio sources may not maximize gamma-ray coincidence.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
K-S tests were used to assess distribution differences. Monte-Carlo simulations were used for opening angle statistics. The lack of CSOs is marginally significant.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 plots gamma-ray fluxes against radio flux density. Figure 2 shows 5 GHz VIPS images for likely candidates. Figure 5 plots the distribution of core-to-jet ratio. Figure 6 shows brightness temperature distributions. Figure 7 shows jet opening angles and bending. Table 1 summarizes the candidate EGRET sources. Table 3 provides core sizes and brightness temperatures.

Three Takeaways
1. EGRET blazars have higher Doppler factors, indicated by higher core fractions and brightness temperatures. 2. Radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux at low flux levels. 3. Future gamma-ray source selection should prioritize high core fractions and large opening angles.
